The ledger doesn't tell you what Tre sees when he walks past the Baylight fence line every day, or whether the new money coming into Jack London feels like it's for him or just passing through. plan.focus: The gap between Jack London's business growth and the displacement pressure on the workers who power it — told through Tre Mingo and the people on the ledger at the Port, Green & Gold, and Anchor Build.
plan.why: Every business on this slice is expanding — the Port added workers, Anchor Build is up 13.7%, the taverns are holding — but the engine colors show people watching storefronts paper over and doing rent math that doesn't work. That tension is the economic story of Jack London right now: who gets to stay when the neighborhood finally turns.

targets.question: When you walk past the Baylight fence line on your way to the gate, do you feel like that development is for you — or just happening around you?
targets.basis: Tre Mingo is the named Port worker on the ledger, the longest-tenured voice on this slice, and the natural entry point into the Port's growth and its meaning for the people who work there.

targets.question: Anchor Build is up 13.7% and you're managing 181 workers — are the projects you're building keeping Jack London affordable for the people on your crews, or pricing them out?
targets.basis: Marguerite Salcedo is the managing partner of the construction firm on the ledger; she holds the clearest view of whether the building boom serves the existing workforce or the incoming one.

targets.question: The tavern's doing fine — revenue up, regulars in the seats — but what are you hearing from the people at the bar about whether they can afford to stay in the neighborhood?
targets.basis: Guadalupe Lupe is the bartender at Green & Gold, the spot where the block's workers actually talk; she hears the rent anxiety that doesn't show up on a ledger.

plan.interpretation: The ledger shows a neighborhood that's technically thriving — every named business is growing, hiring, holding revenue. But the engine colors tell a different story underneath: people watching storefronts die, doing rent math that doesn't close, planning weekends around a day game because that's the only affordable escape. The growth isn't fake — it's just not evenly distributed. The question is whether the people doing the work get to share in what they're building, or whether they're building

Milena Coleman did rent math on an envelope and sat back hard — worth asking what the number was and what it means for her staying put
